speakeroldname: Mr. Art Lee (Parliamentary Secretary to Solicitor General):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Solicitor General of Canada
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PARDON FIRST OFFENDERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before commenting on the substance of this bill let me say that the preyious speakers, including the hon. member for St. Catharines (Mr. Parent), spoke of the worth of the private member sponsoring this bill. His worth was made even more evident by the kind words the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) had to say about the hon. member for Simcoe North (Mr. Rynard). I wish to add to what was said. Having prepared some remarks on this bill, and having read some of the previous debates on this subject and previous comments of the hon. members for Simcoe North, I can say that the hon. member has demonstrated a genuine concern for young people. He is concerned about reforms in our criminal justice system. That being so, I join others in this House in congratulating the hon. member for Simcoe North for introducing the bill. It has given us an opportunity once more to discuss this subject.

When the Criminal Records Act was introduced, it was pointed out by the solicitor general of the day that it did not necessarily represent the best legislation which could be devised on this subject. It was envisaged that after some experience with the new act, modifications of substance might be found desirable. As the former solicitor general mentioned last year in debate on a private member's bill introduced by the hon. member for Simcoe North in substantially the same form and content, the ministry has recognized the need for a complete revision of legislation, and only other priorities in the legislative program delayed the introduction of substantial amendments during the last session.
The proposed legislation, prepared by the ministry, is in its final stages and should be introduced during the next session. Unfortunately the details of the bill cannot be revealed at present, but the principal areas in which the department is working can be discussed today. I want to assure the House that some of the comments made here today, particularly those by the hon. member for Simcoe North, will be taken into consideration by the minister, because they will help us to improve this important legislation. It goes without saying that the minister agrees with the hon. member for Simcoe North and others who have spoken that the Criminal Records Act has been inadequate and that amendments are necessary.
When this act was passed on June 11, 1970, it was the first occasion on which a Canadian parliament had passed a law to relieve specifically convicted persons from their criminal records. Before that date there were the provisions of the Criminal Code, section 683, which authorized the governor in council to grant pardon, whether free or conditional. There were also the provisions of the letters patent establishing the role of the Governor General of Canada; they empower the Governor General to grant pardons. But there was no legislation dealing specifically with the criminal records of those pardoned convictions.
The Criminal Records Act has been a first attempt to continue and to limit acccess to judicial and criminal records. It was recognized at that time as a major step forward. On the other hand, it was also recognized that this law, like most new laws, would meet unforeseen difficulties and contain unforeseen deficiencies which would only come to light with practical experience. Many of these difficulties and deficiencies have now been identified, and members opposite have mentioned some of them.
Since its implementation the Department of the Solicitor General has been conducting a complete review of this legislation and working on amendments to the act. Moreover, the previous minister and departmental officials have discussed these proposals with the provinces, as they do affect the provinces very closely. I know that it is the earnest hope of my minister to have our proposals with respect to the legislation finalized very shortly, with a bill to be introduced into this House in the upcoming session this fall. I want to assure hon. members that their suggestions and comments here this afternoon will be examined by the minister, and I am confident that they will prove useful in preparing that bill.
March 29, 1977

Experience with the Criminal Records Act during the six years since its passage has indicated a number of deficiencies. First of all, a pardon granted under the act has not been effective, as we had hoped, in protecting an ex-inmate from discrimination and in helping him to reintegrate into society. That was the principal goal of the bill.
As a member of the subcommittee on penitentiaries, I can certainly confirm this conclusion, and in fact it may well be one of the major contributors to recidivism. One of the principal challenges facing the ex-inmate is finding a job. Very often he is faced with closed doors due to his criminal record. While the law that is in force now provides help to the ex-inmate in respect of employment by the federal government, and employment in areas which fall within the jurisdiction of the federal government, it does not help in areas that fall within the jurisdiction of provincial governments. As most hon. members know, the greater proportion of jobs and employment in this country falls within the jurisdiction of provincial governments' labour legislation and general legislation. Although a person is holding a pardon, he cannot deny his pardoned conviction or criminal record, so that right from the application for employment he is almost in no better position than a convicted person without pardon.
When the present statute was passed in 1970, it was hoped the provinces would follow our example by passing similar laws to protect ex-inmates. Little has been done in that area. I believe British Columbia and Ontario have legislation limiting access to criminal records of pardoned persons, or on discrimination which could be practised against ex-inmates. As a result, under the amendments we are now preparing, we hope to make pardons applicable at all jurisdictional levels, federal and provincial. So far we have put proposals to the provinces and they are generally in agreement.
Another deficiency was found in the present legislation with respect to its effectiveness. While a pardon in accordance with the act renders a conviction void, and while it removes any disqualification attached to the conviction of those affected in society, and that is what the statute says, it does not prevent provincial or municipal authorities from revealing the fact of the conviction.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH DEPARTMENT OF EMPLOYMENT AND IMMIGRATION, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on February 28 when I spoke briefly on this bill I mentioned the high unemployment and the sums of money being dumped into make-work programs which are not giving the relief to the unemployed that they should. The unemployment problem has to be attacked on a long-term basis. All the make-work projects are doing is giving band-aid treatment to the festering sore of over one million people unemployed in Canada today.
The minister has stated that if this bill passes there will be a saving of $200 million. I want to know if the government will use this money to pay agents for the sale of nuclear reactors in some country still unnamed, or if it will use the money to stimulate the economy, especially in high unemployment areas, by establishing industries there.
The government has tried to encourage people from one area of this vast country of ours to relocate to the west and north where jobs for skilled tradesmen are available. This program has failed completely. In many cases it has resulted in broken families because the bread winner sometimes does not have the funds to return home when the job is finished. This state of affairs has existed for quite sometime and the government has spent vast sums of money to relocate people right across the country through a program that is just not working.
The federal government has an annual buy of $8 billion, yet some of that money is spent outside Canada. I feel that if more
4454

March 29, 1977
Employment and Immigration
of it were spent in this country for goods produced here, as well as some of the $200 million that the minister claims will be saved by changing the qualifying period for unemployment insurance from eight weeks to 12 weeks, then industries could be established in high unemployment areas to produce the goods required by the government.
The change in the qualifying period from eight weeks to 12 weeks in order to qualify for unemployment insurance will not make any difference to many people who live in remote areas of Canada. It is compulsory for everyone who is gainfully employed to pay unemployment insurance. In many cases, however, people in remote areas who have gone out to work on pipelines or hydro projects and then returned to their isolated communities have found themselves discriminated against. They have to make their contribution to unemployment insurance, but when it comes time to collect they are left out in the cold because there is not a manpower centre in their area to which they can report.
I should like to refer to the case of a constituent of mine whose claim was turned down by the Unemployment Insurance Commission. A letter from the commission said that a person who lives in a remote area and has not made himself available for a job does not therefore qualify for unemployment insurance benefits. I believe this is discrimination. Whether people live in Montreal or Shamattawa, Manitoba, if they contribute to unemployment insurance they should be able to collect. Apparently the department does not agree. My constituent appealed his case on the grounds that Shamattawa is an isolated village accessible only by air. The nearest unemployment insurance office is in Thompson, Manitoba, over 200 miles away. The Unemployment Insurance Commission found that my constituent had not been actively seeking work. Mr. Speaker, for him to report to the Manpower centre in Thompson to see if there were any jobs would cost around $200 or $300. This is only one case that I cite tonight. Mr. Speaker.
In other cases when someone has made their way to the Canada Manpower centre they have found that the jobs available were for skilled workers only. Skilled or unskilled, contributions are compulsory, but there is no difference in the amount of benefits.
Considering the complaints of people in remote areas whose applications for unemployment insurance have been turned down flat, even though they have contributed to the program handsomely, I suggest it is high time the government examined seriously the legislation before the House, since changing the qualifying period from eight to 12 weeks will put people in remote areas in an even worse position than they are in now.
We are debating this bill under the guillotine, and I never guessed I would speak on the unemployment insurance bill with the gun of closure pointing at my head.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party

Shame!
(Mr. Smith (Churchill).)

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH DEPARTMENT OF EMPLOYMENT AND IMMIGRATION, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, people are concerned about this question and they have no voice except that of their member of parliament. That is why I wanted to draw attention to the plight of people in remote areas, people who will not benefit from unemployment insurance.
Let me mention the complaints of another constituent. Having contributed to unemployment insurance for ten years, this chap was laid off on December 9, 1976, owing to excessive loss of time from illness over which he had no control. On December 1, 1976, he decided to move from the city to the country, since housing was cheaper and living costs lower in the country. But he decided to remain on the roll of those actively looking for employment in order to remain qualified for unemployment insurance. When he applied for unemployment insurance, he was turned down because he had moved from the city without first contacting the UIC office. This chap was unemployed for approximately two months and could not obtain benefits because he had not notified the people at the UIC office that he was moving out of the city. In the meantime, he had no income and, with a wife and child to feed, he found ends hard to meet.
Ultimately he appealed to the unemployment insurance commission in Winnipeg. He felt he had been discriminated against. He had contributed to UIC, but had not informed the people at the UI office of his move, and therefore was disentitled. This experience left a distasteful impression with him. He was out of a job until January 25, 1977. I ask, is there one rule for country folk and another for city dwellers? It seems to me that urban and rural contributors to the unemployment insurance fund make essentially the same sort of contributions.
At present, if people happen to move from the city and do not notify the UIC counsellor or satisfy him, they can be disqualifed at the stroke of a pen. I bring this to the minister's attention as one small example of what can happen. I am sure many hon. members, especially on the opposition side, could refer to letters showing how concerned our people are about unemployment insurance.
It has been said that some people, through a variety of means, have ripped off the unemployment insurance fund for many years. I was appalled to learn that some Canada Manpower offices with respect to which there have been complaints of fraud have been trying to cover up these frauds. I understand that at many Canada Manpower offices the manager has said to the employees, "Let us keep the lid on; we do not want any more complaints about overpayments because such complaints embarrass the minister". I know in one instance instructions were issued to counsellors to the effect that they were to keep quiet about any discrepancies they found and not bring them out in to the open. This is wrong. If the unemployment insurance program is in a mess, that should be exposed. Changing the eligibility period from eight weeks to 12 will not cut down on cheating. If cheaters found a way to cheat under the eight week system, they will find a way to cheat once the qualifying period is 12 weeks.
I raise another point. I find it appalling that many people who can hold down big jobs during the summer, when they
March 29, 1977

may earn perhaps $1,200 or $1,000 per month, can, once they leave a job, automatically collect unemployment insurance. That is totally against my concept of what unemployment insurance should be. I think the program was set up to be an insurance plan. It was not a plan to which one contributes and from which one withdraws one's contributions when one is not unemployed in the traditional sense. In other words, certain people contribute to the plan, and some people try to rip the plan off. It should not be this way.
I am sure the minister will agree when I suggest that there is no proper unemployment insurance counselling in many remote areas of Canada. In order to qualify for a job, even on a make-work program, you must register with a Canada Manpower centre. But it is impossible for people in remote areas such as northern Manitoba to register. I asked the minister to consider this when make-work projects in remote areas are contemplated. The criteria should take such considerations into account.
We have quite a number of make-work projects available to us. I refer to the LIP program, LEAP, the Canada Works, and Young Canada Works programs, among others. Many of these projects are governed by separate guidelines, and separate project officers are in charge of them. I draw the minister's attention to this fact, because this situation has created difficulties in the remote areas of Canada. Many communities which qualify for programs like Canada Works, Young Canada Works, and LIP are in the remote regions of the country, sometimes well over 200 flying miles from the nearest urban community. Project officers in charge of each make-work program are forced to make separate trips to these communities and the net result is that the people of the communities are not given the service they should get. They become confused as to which program any program officer may represent. All they know is that he works for the government and has money to hand out in areas of high unemployment.
In some instances unemployment runs as high as 20 per cent. If you include communities not covered by unemployment insurance statistics-I am thinking of native communities-unemployment can run between 70 per cent and 75 per cent. The increase in the qualifying period from eight to 12 weeks really will not affect certain northern communities, because many who live on reserves will not qualify for unemployment insurance. However, those who hold permanent jobs and have contributed to unemployment insurance over the years will, I am sure, welcome this type of legislation. Once the proper amendments are made to this legislation during the committee stage, I will have no problem supporting it.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH DEPARTMENT OF EMPLOYMENT AND IMMIGRATION, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am delighted to take part in this debate on Bill C-27, which I feel is one of the most important pieces of legislation with which we could deal as parliamentarians.
Employment and Immigration
Throughout the years, we have come to realize the serious defects which result from the totally unacceptable division between the manpower services and the unemployment insurance services. Mr. Speaker, the two objectives of this bill can easily be summarized. The first one is to integrate the Department of Manpower and Immigration with the Unemployment Insurance Commission, and the second is to amend the unemployment insurance scheme. Mr. Speaker, the Department of Manpower and Immigration has developed considerably over the past few years or, I should say, over the past 15 years or.so.
It will be easily recalled that at that time, during the 60s, the vocational, employment and mobility programs and most of all the new job creation schemes like the Local Initiative, Canada Works and Young Canada Works programs did not exist. These new programs and this new policy have given a tremendous importance to the Department of Manpower. The unemployment insurance program has also taken a tremendous expansion since 1970.
Besides, in my opinion, and I say this as a government member as well as a private member, we then made an error which seems rather serious to me. We felt that it was normal that unemployment insurance benefits be granted to as many people as possible and at the highest rate possible, while forgetting that the basic objective of this unemployment insurance benefit program was to help genuinely unemployed people, those who had held a regular job and not temporary work. In any event, I will come back a little later to my comments on this second part of the unemployment insurance legislation. I would like first of all to revert to the first objective which is to join the services provided by the Department of Manpower and the Unemployment Insurance Commission. Mr. Speaker, I think there is basically one main reason warranting this new integration.
I hope this integration will considerably improve some services which are, we must admit, very deficient in many cases. Indeed, Mr. Speaker, I think that those services can and must be improved because, first, this integration will enable us to rationalize the present system of local UIC and Department of Manpower offices. Second, I hope this integration will change most service offices into integrated centres which will provide the public with all the services of both organizations. Third, Mr. Speaker, I hope this measure will make for faster and more systematic information about available employment services. Finally, Mr. Speaker, I do hope this measure will simplify the paperwork requested from the client. It is important, in my opinion, to point out that this integration will result in a unified administration and ultimately in offering under one roof services which are related.
If I may mention a case which concerns me more particularly, for it is the case of my own riding, Mr. Speaker, I must say that the constituents of Lapointe are fortunate enough to have a Canada Manpower office, but when they have unemployment insurance problems they must go to the next municipality which is at least ten miles away from my riding.
80012-4l/2

March 29, 1977
Employment and Immigration
Of course, this entails substantial disbursements which people who draw unemployment insurance benefits or who are unemployed are not able to cope with. In the constituency of Lapointe, we had an unemployment insurance and a manpower office a few years ago but owing to the centralization of unemployment insurance services and to automation, two separate offices were established. I am very happy that this bill provides for the reunification of these services not only in the same town but in the same building, which eliminates the injustice my constituents had to suffer.
As a matter of fact, Mr. Speaker, I think that most of the time those who have employment problems also have unemployment insurance problems which cannot be solved by telephone calls. Many people communicate with UIC officials and obtain answers which in some way are not translated into facts. But when a citizen has the opportunity to meet UIC or Canada manpower officials and submit his problems to them I think the individual would be liable to obtain better service and could hopefully solve his problems in a more appropriate manner.
Mr. Speaker, I think this first objective does not meet with too much disagreement among members of the House, whatever their political stripe. I think we have come to accept that integration and harmonization of services even if it must be recognized that it is going to represent in fact perhaps an adaptation that will take a few months, if not years, and perhaps outlays for the location or the integration of services that may temporarily require outlays that could be substantial but that would be justified by the objectives sought.
Mr. Speaker, the second part of the bill generally contains more controversial aspects and I think the second aspect of the bill which concerns changes in unemployment insurance as such is also justified. I would like to say a few words about it because it is easy to take refuge in silence, to say once the bill is passed that one voted because one was on the government side because one had to follow the party line, and people often try to go and get votes on both sides of the fence, believing that the opinion of someone who tries to be on both sides is better than someone who tries to take a clear stand against a bill. I consider that as a legislator, a representative of a constituency in Canada, my first responsibility is to express my point of view on this bill and if my views at times might not to be shared by some of my voters or some of my colleagues on either side of the House, I think my colleagues will have a lot more reason to blame me for not expressing my opinion than trying to put my view before the House.
Mr. Speaker, first I think that the bill which provides for an increase in the number of weeks from eight to twelve can be justified, and I will give a few reasons of my own.
I know it is so, Mr. Speaker, because I come from a riding where the unemployment rate is substantial, much too high, unacceptable, so everyone says. But we must ask ourselves if we will solve the difficult and complex problem of high unemployment by reducing benefits.

I believe the difference between eight and 12 weeks could not affect to a considerable extent the person who is really out of work and especially those who are eligible for unemployment insurance benefits. My idea of unemployment insurance and the relevant legislation may not necessarily be shared by all my colleagues but I am not reluctant to state that I think it is somewhat abusive, if not worse, for persons to work eight weeks and then draw 52 weeks of unemployment insurance benefits. It is very well for the person receiving such benefits to accept them, to claim them and to resent those who are trying to take them away. But on the other hand, I must not represent only the unemployed in my riding, who are going through hard times and who need my help, I must also protect the worker who must contribute often excessive sums to unemployment insurance funds which have become totally out of proportion. It is a matter of S3 or $4 billion. It is the worker who must pay, Mr. Speaker.
Certainly, as the member for Bonaventure-Iles-de-la-Madeleine (Mr. Bechard) mentioned, he is indeed lucky to be working but when his salary is almost equal to the benefits of someone else who draws unemployment insurance, he does not seem as lucky, as fortunate. We must also consider the many representations made by workers who say they sympathize with the unemployed; the government must not give him money for not doing anything but rather get him a job, establish job creation programs, training programs; in other words, the government must see to the retraining and reintegration into the labour market of the person who, for some reason or another, not necessarily of his own doing, is out of a job.
I think we made a serious mistake in 1971 because under the pretext of helping those who had problems, we created more serious problems. And we realize today that instead of increasing unemployment benefits in such an extraordinary way, we should have adopted the solution we are proposing today to reallocate the funds of the Department of Manpower to the creation of new jobs, to training and to some other solutions which do not maintain unemployment but help the unemployed worker find a new job.
I admit it is a hard position to take vis-a-vis such regions as Gaspesie, the Atlantic area or even my own riding, Mr. Speaker, but given the present situation we are forced to recognize that despite the fact that idle workers generally benefited from the 1971 legislation it did not bring about valuable solutions because instead of declining the unemployment rate has a tendency to rise. In this context, I submit that as legislators we should try a different approach, always with a view to helping the worker, or rather the unemployed.
Mr. Speaker, every member in the House would recognize that in the unemployed's view, unemployment insurance is a form of social welfare he is entitled to. And since there are social help programs where the federal government and the provinces now contribute 50 per cent each, it is to be expected that, instead of using those perhaps less profitable programs,
March 29, 1977

the unemployed think of the UIC as a source of funds where they often get much more.
Mr. Speaker, we must indeed recognize that there is some basic imbalance when someone who worked for eight weeks can get UIC benefits for up to 50 weeks. Admittedly he may not be responsible for his problem in a number of cases, and society must help him. However I feel that puts quite a burden on the worker, the regularly employed, those who have to pay taxes and consider the situation as somewhat bizarre. They blame us as legislators for finding easy ways out, giving away the money we collect and telling people: Listen, we give you money, but finding jobs is too difficult. I submit the tougher alternative, the one we chose, is our commitment to create jobs. This is not easy because we have programs such as Canada Works, Young Canada Works, the LIP program. The latter has been criticized by some, but to me it is essential and must not only be maintained but increased. The money we will be able to redirect should go to make job programs in slow growth areas such as ours.
So in my view the approach we are considering, however belatedly as I said, appears to be the best. I recognize it is the most difficult and the unemployed may have some difficulty in accepting those four extra weeks, but there is nothing to prevent us from trying. Nothing prevents us from seeing how this legislation will work. There is nothing to prevent us later on from making representations to ministers if we were to find that those four weeks taken away from the unemployed caused irreparable loss, that the unemployed could not indeed find another job, and that he was in a worse situation because this legislation had been enacted. I am not saying at all, Mr. Speaker, that we should absolutely accept this law and enforce it until the end of this parliament. We are here to pass laws and introduce the necessary changes when we realize that they fall short of the aim we had in mind when we enacted them. That is why we are here. If statistics can prove to me that this law is prejudicial to people in financial need, I would be the first one to rise in the House and say: This law, Mr. Minister, does not meet our objectives. Don't listen to the bureaucrats who are saying that it should be amended. As for me, Mr. Speaker, I see this bill as a sincere and real effort by the Minister of Manpower to reintegrate these people on the labour market, to give them some motivation and a sense of work I hope they will be able to recover.
The solution proposed by the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Cullen) when he speaks about work sharing projects is quite original, Mr. Speaker, because workers often tell us: You are not listening to the unemployed. Find an answer to their problem, find them work! And today, in this new legislation we are saying to the worker: You work 40 hours a week, you are protected by your union, by various considerations; you are a good employee, the employer will keep you on a 40 hour basis. Due to economic circumstances, the employer is compelled to lay off a number of workers and he will ask those who work to share with others, instead of working 40 hours a week, they will work only 30 hours and
Employment and Immigration
receive unemployment insurance benefits as a compensatory measure.
Mr. Speaker, this is true socialism which I accept. He who asks those who have more to share with those who have less instead of urging the government to spend the money it has levied from taxpayers or at least who does not rely only on the government to find a solution. I have confidence that the worker will realize that he will be able to help his unemployed workmate and find a solution to his problem. At any rate, this solution seems original to me and I think it is desirable to give it a try.
Mr. Speaker, there is also in this legislation a nonsense, if I may use that word, which will finally be eliminated. During the extended period of unemployment insurance, those who had the guts and the wit to work during four weeks were rewarded by forfeiting all unemployment insurance benefits. This was in my view a most stupid and unacceptable reward since it encouraged those who worked not to do it because they were penalized for so doing. Mr. Speaker, this amendment which would remove the penalty for those who are working for four weeks will certainly be approved unanimously by all hon. members of this House.
However, Mr. Speaker, I suggest this bill is an important step, a retreat from the unemployment insurance legislation which we passed, perhaps too quickly, in 1971. I have the impression and I hope that it will establish a new balance between the worker and the unemployed and that the integration of unemployment and manpower will enable our society to benefit more from the government services which are now available and sometimes badly used.
For my part, Mr. Speaker, I believe that this bill deserves some loyal effort on our part, and I must say to those of my colleagues who have some reservations concerning the increase in the number of weeks from eight to twelve that I will be very happy to listen to their arguments in the committee, and if they have acceptable compromise suggestions to solve this problem, which seems to be perhaps the most controversial aspect of the bill, I am not saying that I will not be prepared to consider them. However, I believe that we must together look for solutions, that we shall find them and that this bill will, at least I hope so, help the population, but most importantly, that it will help find employment for the Canadians who need it, who deserve it as much as those in large centres, and I appeal to the government to find, in the short term, solutions such as Canada Works, for which the budget should be increased because, whatever some people may say, whatever the abuses that we know and deplore, those programs are really useful to the community since they bring a certain well-being to the community and, most important, give back to certain people the incentive to work before finding the permanent employment that they would like to find and that I hope we will be able to offer them as soon as possible.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH DEPARTMENT OF EMPLOYMENT AND IMMIGRATION, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a special pleasure for me to take part in the debate on this bill to amend the Unemployment Insurance Act. I say that

March 29, 1977
Employment and Immigration
because 1 served on the committee in 1971 when the present act was brought into being. We argued long in committee, under the leadership of the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Alexander), that what we are doing today should have been done when the act was originally drafted, namely, that the qualifying period should be 12 weeks instead of the present eight weeks. We argued that we felt it provided a disincentive to work, which in many cases over the years has proven to be true. What we advised then, it has taken the government exactly six years to learn.
Having said that, it seems to me that the timing of the introduction of these amendments to the bill we are now debating could not have been worse. Unemployment in Canada today is high enough to be a crime against humanity; some 932,000 or more people are out of work, the greatest number in the history of Canada. That figure is the equivalent of a city the size of Montreal or Toronto without anyone working. Lives are being disrupted and hopes smashed. It does not help for our Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) to tell students that if they cannot get a job here they should leave the country. The timing could not have been worse. While we agree with what the minister is trying to do, we think he has certainly picked a time which brings into focus all the objections that are being raised on his side of the House and on our side of the House. There are differences of opinion.
The minister is on the horns of a dilemma. He is damned if he does; he is damned if he does not. It seems to me there is a very easy way out of the minister's dilemma, that is, if he would simply agree or indicate that he is prepared to accept the principles laid out in the amendment which the hon. member for Hamilton West suggested we introduce at the proper time. He would then serve the interest of those who think the eight week period should be as it is and of those people who feel that the eight week contribution period is too short.
What did the hon. member for Hamilton West have to say? I would like to read a paragraph of his speech as reported in Hansard of February 1, 1977, when he stated the following:
So as it stands now, because of this government's insensitive and ineffective performance we feel that regional differences must be recognized not in words but in deeds. Accordingly, because of our concern and because of the lack of response by the government, I now advise the House that my party will move an amendment to clause 17. This is in general what we intend to do. We propose the following amendment:
In high unemployment regions, the minister may, with the approval of the governor in council, make regulations.
-lowering from 12 weeks down to a minimum of 8 weeks the number of weeks referred to in subsection 16(1) and 17(2)(a);
-defining high unemployment regions, delineating the boundaries thereof and determining residence and eligibility within such region;
-setting a date of termination for any such regulations-
It seems to me that this is a practical, sensible solution to the minister's dilemma. This is the reason why we in our party are sensitive to the very wide variations in economic conditions across this country of ours. To say there must be one hard and fast set of regulations or an act of parliament, or a section of

an act, to apply rigidly throughout Canada, just does not make any sense. We are trying to argue that for those people who need it, let us make it available to them in the way it should be made available.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH DEPARTMENT OF EMPLOYMENT AND IMMIGRATION, ETC.
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH DEPARTMENT OF EMPLOYMENT AND IMMIGRATION, ETC.
speechtext: There is a necessity for unemployment insurance. Nobody can argue against that. In today's world it prevents much of the hardship that would otherwise fall on the person who loses his or her job. However, I am concerned that the program should not be of such a magnitude that it becomes an undue financial burden on the nation. It seems to me that is exactly what it is becoming. Therefore it becomes self-defeating in terms of employment. I am concerned that it should not become a disincentive to work program. Neither can it be denied that the unemployment insurance program brings relief to municipalities which otherwise would be paying out large sums in welfare payments to keep those people who have no means of earning an income. The then minister of manpower and immigration who at that time piloted this bill through the House, the honourable Bryce Mackasey, argued that, and we agreed it would certainly help.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH DEPARTMENT OF EMPLOYMENT AND IMMIGRATION, ETC.
speechtext: Don't mention his name.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH DEPARTMENT OF EMPLOYMENT AND IMMIGRATION, ETC.
speechtext: We must not lose sight of the fact that unemployment insurance is not a welfare program. As the hon, member who preceded me said, so many people have a misunderstanding of what unemployment insurance is. They feel it is a government annuity, that because you pay into it, therefore somewhere down the line you are entitled to withdraw from it.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH DEPARTMENT OF EMPLOYMENT AND IMMIGRATION, ETC.
speechtext: A good point, Sir.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH DEPARTMENT OF EMPLOYMENT AND IMMIGRATION, ETC.
speechtext:
That is not the case at all. It is this misunderstanding that has led to a lot of the difficulties with the administration of the Unemployment Insurance Act.
Another good point the minister is introducing in this amendment is the remarrying of the Unemployment Insurance Commission and the Department of Manpower and Immigration.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH DEPARTMENT OF EMPLOYMENT AND IMMIGRATION, ETC.
speechtext: Another one of our policies.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH DEPARTMENT OF EMPLOYMENT AND IMMIGRATION, ETC.
speechtext:
That is right. That is another one of our policies, as the hon. member for Hamilton West says. They should never have been separated in the first place. The original act was administered in this very way. This enabled Manpower centres to keep track of those people who were drawing welfare. At that point in time they came to the Manpower centres to pick up their unemployment insurance cheques. If there was a job for them to do, they certainly did not receive their cheques. They took the job or went without unemployment insurance. It seems to me that the minister should look very seriously at reinstituting some such program, especially in urban centres or in rural areas where the density of population warrants it.
March 29, 1977

He should look into instituting a program of distributing unemployment insurance cheques through the Manpower centres as they once did. That may not be an efficient way of doing it, but it would be a way of policing the program. Do not tell me that it does not work. At the time of the mail strike several months ago when the mails were not moving and the unemployment insurance cheques were not getting out, the cheques were delivered to the Manpower centres in various towns and municipalities across the country. They were distributed to the people. They came and picked them up. Another important aspect which came to light at that time was that there were a lot of so-called unemployed who did not come to pick up their cheques. I have a strong suspicion that they were the ones who certainly did not deserve them.
The present program and the regulations under which it operates lack something in efficiency. It employs many, many hundreds of public servants who are doing an excellent job. I have no quarrel with any unemployment insurance officer. When I go to them with a problem, if it is reasonable they listen to me and try to help me out.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH DEPARTMENT OF EMPLOYMENT AND IMMIGRATION, ETC.
speechtext: Unlike the minister.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH DEPARTMENT OF EMPLOYMENT AND IMMIGRATION, ETC.
speechtext:
I would not say that. The minister is a good fellow. He is a good friend of mine. As I said, he is on the horns of a dilemma here. I have pointed a way out of that dilemma. I hope the minister takes note of the amendment we are suggesting. While there are hundreds of people doing the work that I have mentioned, there also are over 260 members of parliament, as well as their staffs, to make this program work. I do not know how many times over the years we are plagued to death with people coming into our constituency offices or writing to us or phoning us with unemployment insurance problems. It is time to look at the way the regulations and the administrative procedures are set up. We are acting as ombudsmen for the program.
There are many examples of discrimination in the program. I do not know how to correct them. It is not my job to find out the way, but I will point out some of the things that are wrong about it. Often I find two people doing the same kind of work-working for the same farmer in this instance-who are laid off at the same time. Both apply for unemployment insurance. One draws it without any question, but the other one is called in for an interview and there is some excuse found for disentitling that person. It is most frustrating to try to explain why one draws it under the same conditions while the other is denied benefits. I do not know what the answer is, whether it is a more solid administrative program, but that is what is happening.
The appeal procedures require some changes. 1 am pleased to see that claimants now have a right to appeal to the umpire, regardless of the number of the board of referees who rule against the claimant. As it now stands, if there is a unanimous decision to withhold unemployment insurance, that person has no right to appeal to the umpire. Under the bill that is to be changed, and that is good.
Employment and Immigration
I want to draw to the minister's attention and to the attention of his officials the case of a young woman living in Cayuga by the name of Mary Termorshuizen. She appealed her case and went to the board of referees. She was given only five minutes' time before the board to state her case. As a matter of fact she was given no opportunity to make a statement and no opportunity to ask questions of the board of referees as to why the insurance officer made the decision in the way he did. In this case the lady in question had her employer agree to come to make representation on her behalf. The date had to be changed. The employer was not informed of the change of date and, as a result, was not able to support her before the board of referees. She was exceedingly frustrated and terribly upset by the offhand manner in which her case was heard by the board of referees.
One other point that has arisen and has been drawn to my attention many times is with regard to the sickness benefit claim. It seems that when the sickness benefit claim is established first, it continues to run continuously until it expires, whether or not the claimant draws on it. I have heard of instances of claimants being sick, having a doctor's certificate and filing for unemployment insurance. One claimant received payments for two or three weeks, whatever it may have been. When she felt better, the doctor allowed her to go back to work, but he warned her that her illness might flare up again and she might have problems. In fact a month or two later she was sick again and had to be hospitalized. She was off work for a considerable period of time. Later she was most frustrated to find that her claim had expired, even though she did not draw on it continuously since her first sickness. I wrote to the minister about it and I understand his officials realize that this is an injustice that should be corrected. I sincerely hope it will be.
Now I want to draw to the minister's attention some of the strange disentitlement procedures to which my attention has been drawn from time to time. First of all, there is a group of people who are of a certain age at which they find it most difficult to find work, people in their fifties and sixties.
I have a letter here from a lady who lives in Delhi, Mrs. Elizabeth Kora. She is 59 years old. She has been told that she must go out and hunt for work each day or make so many searches a week or a month, which she does. But in no way will anybody hire a woman who is 59 years old. It is ridiculous even to ask for this in the first place. However, she fulfils the conditions, and yet they say she is not looking for work seriously enough and she does not qualify. This has happened to her for four successive years. Each time this person is harassed by the UIC people and told she is not looking for work seriously. I do not know on what basis these people are sought out to be investigated. I will return to that later. This is one area where I think the program should be reviewed. 1 am referring to the method of disentitlement.
Another class of people who are having difficulty drawing benefits and keeping their claims active are people who drive

March 29, 1977
Employment and Immigration
school buses. They are in a special category. They work during the school year, but when the school is on holidays, they do not work. Because they have been paying into the plan, they file for unemployment insurance benefits. Like everybody else, they must make a search for work. But who will give work to a school bus driver who, they know, in two months time will be back on the job driving the school bus? So I wonder whether or not these people should be forced to pay into a plan when they have no hope of collecting from it. Should there not be some means by which they might draw minimal benefits for a certain number of weeks?
Another matter that concerns me is retroactive disentitle-ment. I am referring to claimants who file for benefits, draw benefits, and then suddenly receive a letter saying, "Sorry, you are disentitled" after having been interviewed and it having been found that they were not looking for work or are disentitled for some other reason. These people are often disentitled not at the time when they were discovered to be not looking for work but retroactively, starting a month or two before then. The claimant then finds that not only is she not receiving the benefit but she is being asked to pay back benefits that she had received until that time. It seems to me that there is something the matter with a system that does that. I can go along with a program that disentitles a person for proper reasons, but to disentitle a person retroactively does not make sense because in all that time the cheques have been drawn in good faith, cashed, and spent, and the person has no funds from which to make the repayment.
Another group of people who require special attention are those who work seasonally in agriculture. They are disentitled most often. They are on their own. They have no union to represent their complaints and to plead their case before the insurance officer. They are easy to disentitle. Many of the same persons in this kind of work are disentitled year after year while, as I pointed out earlier, their co-worker on the job draws benefits without any questions being asked. It is discouraging, to say the least, and many people leave or refuse to take seasonal agricultural work because of the difficulty they have in collecting unemployment insurance and because they are forced to pay into the fund in any case. As a result, that type of worker is rapidly disappearing as a source of labour to harvest farm crops.
I suggest to the minister that we revert to a procedure which was used under the old act under which there was an opting out provision. The worker had the privilege of signing a paper saying that he or she did not wish to make contributions and therefore to draw benefits. All they needed was to sign the paper and the privilege was granted. Believe me, that could remove a lot of headaches and problems for the unemployment insurance program which arise in the area that I represent. I have mentioned this problem before in other speeches in the House, and I have spoken to the minister and to his parliamentary secretary. It seems to me it is worth considering, especially in the case of temporary employment.
I wonder also what directives are sent down through the pipeline to the unemployment insurance officer regarding the

disentitlement of certain people. How is person A selected for disentitlement while person B doing the same job is not? Is it done on a random basis? How do they select those people? When it happens to the same person year after year, as I pointed out in my example a few minutes ago, it becomes frustrating and most difficult to understand. How are claimants selected for investigation?
Before concluding I should like to suggest most strongly to the minister that certain trades, professions or occupations be given special treatment under the act. I refer this time to fishermen. I have colleagues in the House who come from the east and west coasts of this country. I, however, represent a fairly extensive freshwater fishing industry. Fishermen in my area can only fish during a certain time of the year, and they have difficulty qualifying for unemployment insurance under the rigid rules of the present program. At the time the act was passed in 1971 the then minister showed us that consideration was being given to a special type of program tailored to meet the fishing occupation. I ask the minister now whether consideration is still being given to that matter, and why in the world this program has not been implemented after six long years? It seems to me that the proposal should be resurrected and considered to see if we cannot put it into effect because some of these people are suffering.
I began my speech by condemning the unfortunate timing of this bill amending the Unemployment Insurance Act when unemployment is so high and the cost of the unemployment insurance program is ruining the country because of the extensive amounts of money that have to be put in the fund from the public purse. It is simply not actuarially sound. The fact is that too many people are not able to find work and, as has been said over and over again in the House, the responsibility lies squarely on the shoulders of the government.
Those are some of the thoughts I have on the program, and I sincerely hope that the minister and his officials will pay some attention to the complaints I have registered with respect to the disentitlement procedures.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH DEPARTMENT OF EMPLOYMENT AND IMMIGRATION, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to take part in this very important debate on a bill that could have important repercussions on our economy as it will affect many people. This bill contains some positive aspects, and in the five or six minutes that are left to me tonight I would like first to deal with the positive aspects of the bill and tomorrow, or the next time the bill will be debated, I shall mention some effects that some provisions of the bi|l could have on a sector of the population in slow development areas with a high unemployment rate.
Of course, the most positive aspect of the bill is the integration of Canada Manpower services and unemployment insurance offices. I think this integration is essential to any radical change in the administrative structure of unemployment insurance. I think that what we are trying to correct and to re-establish in the unemployment insurance system is the
March 29, 1977

credibility of the program. The minister mentioned it several times and I must say that when we talk about restoring balance between what is paid into the unemployment insurance fund and allowances paid by the program, it seems sound in principle, but when you want to put it into practice you realize that there are some distortions and there might be bad effects in some areas of the country.
But I consider that the integration of those two services might be the basis of any important reform. I think that to re-establish a balance between the amount paid in unemployment insurance premiums and the benefits paid under the program, in other words, if we want to re-establish the credibility of the system, we shall not do it by eliminating people from the rolls or changing the qualifying period or the benefit structure. What happened in 1971 when the two programs were amalgamated is that we could not issue the cheques.
And since it is a complex program dealing with a great number of people, the administration of the Unemployment Insurance Commission in 1971 and at the beginning of 1972 was standing on the defensive before public opinion, because there were some obvious cases in the country, in some areas, especially in my constituency where some nasty demonstrations took place because some people had to wait two or three months for an unemployment insurance cheque.
An effort was made to have a much more effective delivery of cheques and services to customers. What happened is that by making unemployment insurance effective, some extraordinary cases of abuse were made possible and not only abuse but also misuse. In other words, the program is misused. The employers as well as the unemployed or workers are responsible. I say that anyone living in an area such as mine knows that not only since 1971 but for a long time the unemployment insurance program had given rise to abuses by employers and employees from a theoretical point of view. I shall return later on during my speech to what I think generally, that this scheme is not more abused than others where public and private moneys are also involved. But while trying to improve the scheme, we have made it easier for those who want to abuse it. There has been a progression and a multiplication of efforts, so that we must now deal with an entirely new clientele which depends on unemployment insurance benefits.
This clientele includes a number of people who I feel have a legitimate right to receive these benefits, at least in the sense that they are needy. The fact that they are needy is not too serious, provided they can get public money. This clientele includes also a group of people who could have been otherwise integrated into the labour force but who, because of a program such as the unemployment insurance program, together with the other social legislation which was introduced in the late sixties and early seventies, have found it impossible to secure stable employment within far away communities and regions.
But whatever happened, Mr. Speaker, it is impossible to go back to 1971, we are in 1977, and when we have given something to certain people and we try to take it back, this has political and sociological consequences that should be closely examined. And in my opinion, the major problem of unem-
Adjournment Debate
ployment insurance at the present time is one of credibility, and I am ready to say that such a problem exists, even in high unemployment regions like my own. People see the program as a means which can allow people who do not want to work to depend on the public for their living. But the problem is administrative, not only in the sense that we should change something here and there, but also that we need a radical change in the whole administrative structure of unemployment insurance. This is why I believe that Bill C-27, at least in the sense that it aims at integrating both services, is important, because in my opinion, we would need, in specific manpower areas, an employment catalogue which would be up to date, perhaps with a review every two or three months, to show the claimants when they come to ask for unemployment insurance benefits. There is no reason not to have a system telling us immediately whether or not there is employment in that area. There is no reason for not having invented until now a sensitive and humane administration which could tell the claimant as soon as possible: We think that there are jobs available in the sort of work you do. We are close to such a system with the administrative changes made about two years ago. The bill will be helpful if we want to go further in this direction. Mr. Speaker, I note that it is ten o'clock.
A motion to adjourn the House under Standing Order 40 deemed to have been moved.

subtopic: HEALTH-REPORT ON CONNAUGHT LABORATORIES-ACTION TO MAKE CANADA SELF-SUFFICIENT IN BIOLOGICALS
HEALTH-REPORT ON CONNAUGHT LABORATORIES-ACTION TO MAKE CANADA SELF-SUFFICIENT IN BIOLOGICALS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is by preventive medicine and proper health care that the economic burden of illness will be lightened, and the tragedy and waste of disease and death reduced. In the past, federal governments have taken courageous initiatives and demonstrated wise leadership in sponsoring ambitious programs and projects in the field of health care, and recently the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) has professed the importance of preventive medicine to fight disease and its high costs.
In the effort to practice preventive medicine various immunizing agents and biological products play a very important role. The increase of favourable results in protecting the health of Canadians and others, and in practising good preventive medicine by providing effective, reliable, and sufficient quantities of immunizing agents and biologicals was in great measure thanks to the great work done at the Connaught Laboratories of the University of Toronto. For many of us who had the privilege of studying medicine at that university, our visits and lectures at Connaught were particularly edifying experience, especially when we observed at work the dedicated scientific

March 29, 1977
Adjournment Debate
staff and learned about their many discoveries which contributed so greatly to the protection of health and the fight against disease. Tonight I should like to pay tribute from this place to the dedicated staff and the wise administrators of Connaught Laboratories.
Connaught's history reveals that close co-operation with government produced benefits at all times, not only to the institution but also to Canadians in need. Understanding and co-operation brought excellent results. Unfortunately, since Connaught Laboratories was purchased in 1972 by the Canada Development Corporation, the supply of biologicals in Canada has been found deficient.
As stated by a special committee of the Canadian Medical Association studying the plight of Connaught, the awareness of the dichotomy of purpose which occurs when profits are sought from a purely "biologicals" facility is of major importance. It is a shame and a tragedy for Connaught and for Canada that today health ministries of our country have to turn to foreign suppliers for necessary biological products, whereas in the past Connaught has supplied not only Canada but the world with many necessary biologicals.
Today Connaught has not only failed to make profits for the Canada Development Corporation's shareholders but also is unable to provide Canada with necessary biologicals and many immunizing agents, especially in emergencies. The provincial and federal governments, professing their commitment to preventive medicine, must come to realize the urgent need to provide our country with a self-sufficient biological industry. This, Mr. Speaker, is a national need and not just luxury.
I would therefore like to hear this evening from the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. McRae) whether the minister has already made a study of the special report of the Canadian Medical Association committee recommendation that more funds be made available for research and development for a biological industry, especially for Connaught, and that the motive of profitability not be a priority with the CDC which today controls Connaught Laboratories.

speakeroldname: Mr. Paul E. McRae (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: HEALTH-REPORT ON CONNAUGHT LABORATORIES-ACTION TO MAKE CANADA SELF-SUFFICIENT IN BIOLOGICALS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to associate myself with the hon. member in his support of Connaught Laboratories. As Canadians I think we should all feel a great deal of pride in Connaught and be pleased that the Canadian Medical Association report gave them a good bill of health. The report has been studied in a great deal of detail. I refer particularly to the three national recommendations made by this special committee. It is the general tenor of the recommendations that the government should underwrite the cost of producing biologicals which are essential but which may be financially unprofitable, and that it should also undertake the stockpiling of these items. The recommendations require extensive analysis because of potential long-term impact on the pharmaceutical manufacturing sector which up

to now has been allowed to function in a free market environment.
The federal government has on a number of occasions acted to support the biological industry. For example, the federal government has instituted export controls on beef pancreas glands to insure that Canadian supplies of insulin are available for the production of pharmaceutical products like insulin which are essential for Canadian public needs. The federal government also has programs in which industrial firms producing biologicals are eligible for financial assistance from the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce, and additionally the federal government has worked with provincial governments in developing programs to promote an indigenous biologicals industry by undertaking preferential purchasing policies.
The federal government has also undertaken a health care sector study in which the role of the manufacturers of biologicals will be examined in some depth. Our department has been working closely with the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce on this study which, it is expected, would form a thorough base for the development of long range policies governing the pharmaceutical manufacturing sector. In addition, our officials have been requested to examine the report with a view to determining if there is a need to undertake any more immediate short-term action in order to maintain and foster an indigenous capability to produce biologicals.
One should recognize that the federal government is not a major user of biologicals such as vaccines and that any proposals developed could require extensive consultation with provinces which utilize vaccines in their preventive health programs and may elect to pursue independent policies.
The CMA report also contains recommendations relating to the bureau of biologies and the need to increase staff for the purpose of undertaking both inspection and research. The federal government has recognized the need to maintain regulatory controls over biological products, and in both 1976 and 1977 additional man-years were granted by the Treasury Board for this important function. There have been in addition internal transfers to bolster the biologies control programs. Thus, significant strides toward meeting the concerns of the CMA committee have already been undertaken, and biologies control will continue to receive a high priority in subsequent years. I will of course be pleased to announce any further developments concerning government policies relating to the biologies industry when our studies are completed.

subtopic: THE CANADIAN ECONOMY-REASON FOR FAILURE TO CREATE NUMBER OF JOBS PREDICTED IN LAST BUDGET AND INCREASE IN IMPLICIT PRICE INDEX
THE CANADIAN ECONOMY-REASON FOR FAILURE TO CREATE NUMBER OF JOBS PREDICTED IN LAST BUDGET AND INCREASE IN IMPLICIT PRICE INDEX
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I put two simple questions to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) on March 15. I asked first why, the minister having predicted, as reported in Hansard, during his May 25 budget speech last year that 250,000 jobs would be created, were so few actually produced? In the same budget the minister indicated that inflation, based on the implicit price index,
March 29, 1977

would be at 9 per cent in 1976, whereas it actually turned out to be 9.3 per cent, notwithstanding the government's so-called anti-inflation program which included controls. Second, 1 asked why the increase in the implicit price index, not the CPI, should have occurred when growth was disappointingly slow, as reflected by the poor employment record of this administration? As a rule, if the government fouls up growth in the economy, it can at least boast that inflation is lower. But this bunch of amateurs have combined increasing unemployment with rising prices.
When the Minister of Finance introduced the May budget, we challenged the government's inadequate job creation projections and pointed out that a goal of 250,000 new jobs was no goal at all, considering that there were 350,000 known new entrants to the labour force last year. At that time, on May 27 last year, as reported at page 13,898 of Hansard we predicted, and I quote:
... that the government is following a budgetary policy which may well add 50,000 more people to the unemployment rolls which are already at the highest level of the last 15 years.
That was last May. Today we know that one million Canadians are out of work, the actual number of new jobs created was less than 50 per cent of those anticipated, and prospects of the jobless for finding work grow dimmer day by day. Why, Mr. Speaker?
The government is fond of blaming external circumstances, international conditions, for its problems at home. We are told that the reason for our soaring unemployment and disappointing levels of job creation is the economic slowdown common to all OECD nations. On the other hand, it says that those very same countries are causing Canada's inflation. That is utter balderdash. Just look at the facts.
Take the United States, for example, the biggest of the OECD countries and our main trading partner. Last year their gross national product increased in real terms by 6.3 per cent, compared with our paltry 4.6 per cent. The Conference Board in the current year predicts that the American increase in terms of real growth will be 4.8 per cent, compared to Canada's increase of 2.9 per cent. Also, consider inflation. Last year the American implicit price index went up a mere 5.1 per cent, as compared with the 9.3 per cent in Canada, the increase to which I just referred. In the current year, according to Conference Board projections, the Canadian over-all inflation rate will be 7.2 per cent, compared with the American rate of 5.3 per cent.
Let us consider the most important question of unemployment. The Conference Board anticipates that in the current year average unemployment in this country will be at 7.9 per cent, as compared with the anticipated American unemployment rate of 7.1 per cent. The United States not only has less national unemployment than in this country, but less regional unemployment. In our eastern provinces we have levels of almost 10 per cent to almost 15 per cent. However, when we compare the New England states to the eastern provinces in this country, we find that the New England states have sustained consistently lower unemployment rates than their
Adjournment Debate
counterparts in Canada. Even if slow growth was international, the response to that slowdown is a matter of domestic responsibility.
One of the New England states, New Hampshire, is sustaining an unemployment rate in the 3 per cent range, well below that of our eastern provinces, including Quebec which has an unemployment level of almost 10 per cent. Surely this proves that government's response to external or other pressures does in truth make a difference, contrary to what the Minister of Finance may claim.
New Hampshire is a state that is noted for its tight fisted control over government spending, low taxes, reasonable labour costs, and a hospitable climate for business, not hostile as we have developed in this country under the Trudeau administration. The result is jobs for their residents, not people walking the streets without jobs and a UIC cost of $4 billion to $5 billion per year such as we have in this country.
Why have we not done better? Is it really because of so-called international phenomena over which we apparently have no control, or is it because we simply have not taken the right steps at home? It would appear really to be because this administration has adopted fiscal and financial policies which have put a stranglehold on the economy, weakened confidence, and penalized economic expansion, with the resultant high unemployment.
This brings us to the second question. Why has our implicit price index for 1976 risen to 9.3 per cent despite the efforts of the AIB and the other so-called anti-inflation programs? Again we find that we have fared much worse than our neighbours. The GNP deflator, a more all-encompassing index of price movements through our economy, is nearly twice as high as it is in the United States, which has no controls. I ask the same question again: why?
