The hon. member had his seven minutes. I would like my turn. The hon. member said there are 112,000 more jobs between end of February and end of February. The minister did not say what the figures were end of February to end of February. He talked about the average growth of jobs in the economy between the year 1975 and the year 1976.
In the year 1976, the average employed was 9,572,000. In the year 1975 it was 9,363,000, a difference of 209,000, not 112,000. In other words we go from 44 to 84 per cent. That is

March 29, 1977
Adjournment Debate
not a bad performance considering three or four factors that were involved. Export demand was definitely down.
Rather than refer to all OECD countries, the hon. member chose the United States. The expected rate of growth in the OECD countries did not materialize, and remember we are not talking about the difference of 112,000 and 250,000 but 209,000 and 250,000.
The second problem the hon. member constantly has referred to was that government spending was a great factor in our inflation. One of the factors that resulted in somewhat decreased business activities was a cutback in government expenditures that resulted in the cutback in purchases of goods and services, as well as unemployment. The third matter had to do with activities in the business community, particularly in the third quarter of 1976 when there was a significant number of strikes in the construction area.
The point that offset these three factors was the fact that consumer demand was well maintained throughout this whole period. That says something about our internal economy.

subtopic: INDUSTRY-LEARSTAR JET PROGRAM-NUMBER OF ORDERS FINANCED BY CANADIAN EXPORT DEVELOPMENT CORPORATION
INDUSTRY-LEARSTAR JET PROGRAM-NUMBER OF ORDERS FINANCED BY CANADIAN EXPORT DEVELOPMENT CORPORATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question as reported at page 3572 of Hansard was only part of an opposition attempt to find out the details of the actions taken by the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Chretien) concerning the government's purchase of Canadair, its subsequent venture into the manufacture of executive jet planes and the conclusion of sales agreements for such planes.
During the short history of this Lear jet venture the minister has established a pattern of obfuscation and deception which I particularly regret because I have had a high personal regard for the hon. gentlemen up until these recent events. The story started on October 18 last when the minister answered a question of mine, as reported at page 142 of Hansard, concerning the intentions of the government in this matter, by saying:
We have taken no decision yet concerning this proposition which seems extremely interesting and which does not require direct financial intervention by the government.
On November 19, in a semantic dodge, the government, according to an answer given me by the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Andras), had guaranteed a loan of $50 million to Canadair although the question of security for the loan was left unanswered. His words were:
The government decided to make this commitment to guarantee in order to stimulate what we think would be a beneficial venture for Canadair and Canada.
Then the Minister of Trade and Commerce began to get a little careless with the truth. In a speech to the House on February 10, reported on page 2934 of Hansard, he first misled the House by saying, with reference to the Lear jet contract:
Some people felt I was taking a gamble going into that. I remember replying to some questions in this House. I stated that the prospects were not too bad and that I thought we had a good chance of selling 25, 26 or 27.
As I could find no evidence in Hansard to support the fiction of this quotation, I asked him on February 15, having given him notice:
Could he now inform me as to when he made the remarks he claims to have made? The alternative for me will be to assume that he was indulging in witless boasting last Thursday and has attempted to mislead the House.
Not having the parliamentary courage or courtesy to admit an honest mistake, the minister indulged in obfuscation. His answer was:
To be exact, it was on November 2 in reply to the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre. But I did not say then that we had 25, 26 or 27. I was right when I said it was 53.
The truth of the matter, of course, was that on February 10, as reported at page 2934 he had, wittirlgly or unwittingly, misled the House.
On February 15 he not only tried to conceal his misleading of the House but gratuitously offered another untruth, to wit:
... we have already had over 65 orders, and in his intervention of October 18 he said the program was stupid.
He was referring to me at that time.
For a stupid program, I think we have been quite successful.
Neither in my intervention of October 18 nor on any other occasion did I use the words he ascribed to me. A careful examination of my intervention of October 18 would show that the unkindest thing I said then was:
If the cabinet is softheaded enough to approve this funding, can the minister assure the House that he will, first, bring forward supplementary estimates for debate to cover the provision of the funds...
There is no reference there to the program being stupid. To call this government softheaded in business affairs is not even unusual, considering that this is a government which counts it as an example of shrewdness when it only loses $25 million on a reactor deal, or that this is a government which pays agents up to $20 million without knowing who they are or what they do, or that this is a government which, in the Lockheed LRPA deal, showed its maladroitness by continual dickering until it managed to drive the price of the plane up $60 million and get less aircraft for the money. So it is really a truism to apply the word "softheaded" to this government.
The minister has refused to admit his self-evidently misleading statements in the House while ascribing to a member a remark which was never made. As to the financing of Canadair and the LearStar jet 600, we now know that in this deal, one in which there was to be no direct financial intervention on the part of the administration, the government has paid $38 million for Canadair. It has guaranteed a loan of $50 million to Canadair with no security, and it has guaranteed some $114 million to Federal Express, an American would-be purchaser. So we finally have a taxpayer involvement to the tune of $200 million where there was to be no direct financial involvement. That, coincidentally, is the amount I mentioned at the start of all this on October 18.

March 29, 1977

I think it is time that the minister reverted to his former habits, stopped this ill-suited deception and obfuscation, and gave us some straight answers about the current status of the Lear jet deal.

speakeroldname: Mr. Paul E. McRae (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: INDUSTRY-LEARSTAR JET PROGRAM-NUMBER OF ORDERS FINANCED BY CANADIAN EXPORT DEVELOPMENT CORPORATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I might mention in commencing that Canadair has done rather well with this aircraft. There are now 71 orders for it, and another 15 are expected shortly.
The Crown purchased Canadair Limited from its United States parent, General Dynamics Corporation, by exercising an option which had previously been negotiated recognizing a purchase price of $38 million. This payment was made for all notes and shares and was established following a lengthy assessment of the value placed on assets. The sale was closed on January 5, 1976.
The acquisition of Canadair was made at the time that it was decided to proceed with the long range patrol aircraft, a program significant to Canadair on account of the substantial manufacturing offsets which had been negotiated on its behalf. The occasion was therefore seen as a timely one to continue the measures to restructure the Canadian aerospace industry, and followed the earlier purchase of the only other primary airframe manufacturer in Canada the de Havilland company of Toronto.
With these expectations of significantly improved business, the Canadair management took initiatives in seeking a suitable aircraft development program which would exploit more fully the company's potential in design, development, and production. On April 1, 1976, Canadair entered into an option agreement with Mr. William Lear, the designer of many internationally successful products including the Lear jet series of business aircraft. Under the terms of the ensuing agreement, Canadair acquired all the Lear rights and interests in a new multi-purpose business jet identified as the LearStar 600.
Exercise of the option with Lear was made following government approval on November 1, 1976. During the intervening period Canadair had undertaken three fundamental tasks; first, to accumulate sufficient design and engineering research data to define and verify the predicted technical performance
Adjournment Debate
of the aircraft; second, to secure a number of firm sales orders sufficient to justify the launching of the program; and third, to establish the basis upon which the program would be financed.
The Canadair CL-600 Challenger is a twin-engined, multipurpose jet transport aircraft of advanced design. It features a supercritical wing combined with high bypass ratio, turbo fan engines, and a wide body fuselage. This provides for a unique combination of speed, range, fuel economy, payload potential, and passenger comfort, collectively superior to all competing business jets in this class.
Design and development activities are now fully under way at Canadair. Key equipment suppliers have been identified and firm agreements are in place for the initial phase of production. Aerodynamic tests are proceeding satisfactorily and results to date, including those from work conducted in U.S. facilities and subject to independent verification, are confirming the final configuration of the aircraft. A well established market exists for business jets, and expand:ng sales continue to be in evidence even during a period of economic recession. As I have said, Canadair now has firm orders for 71 of these aircraft, with prospects for a further 15.
A recently concluded purchase agreement by Federal Express, a U.S. express cargo carrier, provides for the purchase of 25 cargo version CL-600 Challengers. The value of this order is $131 million, and financing for up to $118 million was approved by the Export Development Corporation during December, 1976.
The Crown is guaranteeing $50 million of the required $128 million debt financing estimated as the peak exposure during the program. Of the balance of $78 million, $20 million is being guaranteed by the Quebec government and the remainder is secured as a pledge on all the company assets. The money is being provided by the Canadian Bank of Commerce and the Provincial Bank of Commerce and the Provincial Bank of Canada in an 80-20 ratio.
Steps are also being taken to reduce the level of risk and financing to be borne by seeking a foreign partner in the program to an approximate level of 20 per cent participation. Air Italia has emerged as the most promising prospect, and has approved an agreement in principle with Canadair as a basis for establishing the program sharing arrangements.
